lead: An alternative fuel changes three things at once: how much carbon it carries per unit of energy, its octane or cetane number, and how it must be stored. India imports most of its crude oil, so energy security and city air push the search for substitutes. A fuel with more hydrogen and less carbon gives less CO₂ per megajoule; a high octane number lets a spark-ignition engine run a higher compression ratio; but a gas fuel may need a 200 bar cylinder. You cannot judge a fuel on one property.
prereq: You need: octane and cetane numbers and knock (Combustion in SI and CI engines).

blocks.text: CNG (compressed natural gas) is mostly methane, 85 to 95 per cent, stored at about 200 bar in steel or composite cylinders. Methane has a research octane number (RON) near 120 and a lower heating value (LHV) of 50 MJ/kg, so a dedicated CNG engine can run a higher compression ratio without knock. It enters as a gas, so it mixes well and makes almost no soot, and it has the lowest carbon per unit energy of any hydrocarbon. The unburnt HC from a CNG engine is mostly methane, which is hard to oxidise and needs a specially coated catalyst; methane is also a strong greenhouse gas, so leaks matter. Delhi’s buses and auto-rickshaws moved to CNG in the early 2000s.

LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) is propane and butane, liquid at a few bar (up to about 8 bar at room temperature), so it stores in a simple tank. Its RON is about 105 and it burns cleanly, with modestly lower CO2 per MJ than petrol. It comes from refineries and from natural gas processing.

blocks.where: n is the moles of CO₂ per mole of fuel (its carbon atoms); M the fuel’s molar mass in g/mol; 44.0 the molar mass of CO₂; LHV in MJ/kg. The result is in kg CO₂ per MJ.

blocks.text: Ethanol has RON about 109 and LHV about 27 MJ/kg, so a litre carries about two-thirds of the energy of petrol. Its large heat of vaporisation cools the charge, which helps against knock but makes cold starting harder. India sells petrol blended with ethanol (E10 and E20); blends need compatible seals and hoses, because ethanol attacks some rubbers and corrodes some metals when water is present. Methanol is similar, but more toxic and corrosive.

Biodiesel is made by transesterification: vegetable oil or animal fat reacts with methanol over a catalyst to give fatty acid methyl esters (FAME) and glycerol. Its cetane number is about 50 to 60 and its LHV about 38 MJ/kg. The oxygen in the molecule cuts soot, CO and HC, but NOx often rises slightly. Raw vegetable oil is not biodiesel: it is far too viscous for an injector.

Other fuels are used in special cases. DME (dimethyl ether) is a gas at room conditions that liquefies at about 5 bar; its cetane number is about 55 and it burns almost without soot. Biogas is 50 to 70 per cent methane with CO2, cleaned before use. Producer gas from burning biomass in limited air is about half nitrogen, with CO and H2; its LHV is only about 4 to 6 MJ per normal cubic metre. Ammonia carries no carbon but ignites poorly and needs a pilot fuel.

sections.h3: Hydrogen, and the fuels side by side

blocks.text: Hydrogen has the highest LHV per kg, about 120 MJ/kg, and no carbon, so burning it gives no fuel CO2, CO, HC or soot. It burns in air from about 4 to 75 per cent by volume, needs a minimum ignition energy about a tenth that of petrol, and has a fast flame. So the design problems are pre-ignition, backfire into the intake and NOx: the flame is hot and the nitrogen comes from the air. Hydrogen engines run lean or use direct injection. It is stored as gas at 350 or 700 bar, or as liquid at about 20 K. Its climate benefit depends on how it is made: from natural gas (grey), with the CO2 captured (blue), or by electrolysis with renewable power (green).

examples.question: Compare the CO<sub>2</sub> per megajoule of petrol, taken as iso-octane C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> (M = 114.2 g/mol, LHV 44 MJ/kg), and methane CH<sub>4</sub> (M = 16.04 g/mol, LHV 50 MJ/kg). CO<sub>2</sub> is 44.0 g/mol.
steps: CO<sub>2</sub> per kg methane: 44.0 ÷ 16.04 = 2.74 kg/kg; per MJ: 2.74 ÷ 50 = 0.0549 kg/MJ.
examples.answer: Petrol gives 0.0701 and methane 0.0549 kg CO<sub>2</sub> per MJ, so methane gives about 22 % less for the same energy.

examples.question: A car has a 60 L (water capacity) CNG cylinder filled to 200 bar at 15 °C. Methane’s compressibility factor there is 0.80 (real density 168 kg/m³). Find the methane mass, its energy, and the petrol volume with the same energy (petrol 0.74 kg/L, 44 MJ/kg).
steps: Real density: 133.9 ÷ 0.80 = 167.4 ≈ 168 kg/m³ (the gas is more compressible than ideal).
Petrol mass with that energy: 503 ÷ 44 = 11.4 kg; volume 11.4 ÷ 0.74 = 15.5 L.
examples.answer: The cylinder holds about 10.1 kg of methane, 503 MJ, the energy of only 15.5 L of petrol; this is why CNG cars carry petrol too.

traps: Calling a hydrogen engine zero-emission: it makes no CO<sub>2</sub>, CO or soot from the fuel, but NOx still forms from the air.
Treating CNG’s HC like petrol HC: it is mostly methane, which an ordinary catalyst barely oxidises and which is a strong greenhouse gas.
Forgetting ethanol’s low LHV: about 27 MJ/kg, so more fuel is needed for the same power.
Calling raw vegetable oil biodiesel: biodiesel is FAME made by transesterification.
Using the ideal-gas law for CNG at 200 bar: it under-predicts the mass by about 20 % (Z ≈ 0.80).

quiz.q: State the main component, RON and storage pressure of CNG.
quiz.a: Mostly methane (85 to 95 %), RON about 120, stored at about 200 bar.

quiz.q: What reaction makes biodiesel, and what are its products?
quiz.a: Transesterification of vegetable oil or fat with methanol over a catalyst; it gives fatty acid methyl esters and glycerol.

quiz.q: Why does ethanol’s high heat of vaporisation help against knock but hurt cold starting?
quiz.a: It cools the charge as it evaporates, lowering the end-gas temperature and so knock; when the engine is cold, the same heat demand leaves too little vapour for the first firings.

quiz.q: A fuel gives 2 mol CO<sub>2</sub> per mol, has M = 32 g/mol and LHV 45 MJ/kg. Find its CO<sub>2</sub> per MJ.
A 100 L hydrogen tank at 700 bar and 15 °C holds gas at 40.2 kg/m³. How much energy does it carry?
quiz.a: Mass 40.2 × 0.1 = 4.02 kg; energy 4.02 × 120 = 482 MJ, about the energy of 14.8 L of petrol.

quiz.q: A hydrogen engine meets no CO<sub>2</sub> or CO limit trouble but fails on NOx. Explain, and give one fix.
quiz.a: Hydrogen burns hot and fast, and the nitrogen and oxygen of the air form thermal NO. Running very lean (λ above about 2) keeps the flame cool enough; otherwise SCR is needed.

quiz.q: Biodiesel lowers soot but may raise NOx. Give the reason for each.
quiz.a: The oxygen in the fuel molecule helps burn the rich core, so less soot forms and more burns out. The same oxygen and a slightly earlier, hotter burn can raise the peak temperature and NO.

beyond: Not for the exam. Studies now compare fuels “well to wheel”, adding the CO<sub>2</sub> of making and moving the fuel to what leaves the tailpipe, and count methane slip with its stronger warming effect. Hydrogen and ammonia engines for trucks and ships are in trials, and flex-fuel cars that run any ethanol blend are being introduced in India. Search next for “well-to-wheel emissions”, “flex-fuel vehicle” and “hydrogen internal combustion engine”.
